start_here.default.q: What is the Start Here page?
start_here.default.a: It is the front door to the C2A2 explorer. It asks three questions in order -- What's this, Who's who, So what -- and hands each to a page that answers it. Nothing here filters, draws, or computes; it is prose and doorways.

start_here.default.q: Where should I begin if I'm new?
start_here.default.a: Start Here. Its first question is deliberately answered twice, by two doors that are a matched pair: the Saying lens asks what the thing says by being the shape it is, and the Doing lens names a structure and the function it makes possible. Neither is a summary of the other. I would read them in that order.

start_here.default.q: How do I get back to the beginning?
start_here.default.a: Click the Start Here tab in the top bar any time -- it's always there.

start_here.default.q: What can I do from the Start Here page?
start_here.default.a: Walk the three sections with pick, next and previous, read or summarise the one you are on, or go through a door: What's it saying, What's it doing, Who's who into the Sociogram, the review cards, or the Summa commentary.

sociogram.graph.default.a: A force-directed graph of the RC Wiki knowledge base: nodes are wiki articles, edges are wikilinks, mentions and shared references. It shows the conceptual neighbourhoods of the thinker traditions and where they connect.

sociogram.graph.default.q: How many nodes are in the Sociogram?
sociogram.graph.default.a: That number moves as the wiki grows, and the figure in the older help text is out of date -- so I will not quote one. Ask me to check the current view and I will read you what it actually reports.

sociogram.graph.default.q: Can I focus on one thinker?
sociogram.graph.default.a: Yes -- use the tradition and category filters on the left to isolate a thinker's conceptual neighborhood, or just ask me to show it.

sociogram.graph.default.q: What do the edge controls do?
sociogram.graph.default.a: They let you show or hide link types and adjust how strongly connected nodes attract each other.

sociogram.graph.default.q: What do the edge types mean?
sociogram.graph.default.a: They distinguish wikilinks, mentions, and shared references, and whether a link crosses categories or stays within one.
A checkbox that isolates one thinker's articles -- Levin, Friston, Hoffman, and so on -- so you can see their neighborhood.
Groupings like Master, Architecture, Agents, and others that organize the wiki by role rather than by thinker.

sociogram.graph.default.q: Can I hold the layout still?
sociogram.graph.default.a: Yes -- use Hold Forces to freeze the graph, and Fit All to recenter everything in view.

sociogram.graph.node_selected.q: How do I read a specific article?
sociogram.graph.node_selected.a: Click any node and its article opens in the side panel. Click an edge instead and both endpoint articles show, one per panel.

sociogram.graph.node_selected.q: What is this article and what can I do with it?
sociogram.graph.node_selected.a: The right panel shows the selected node's article as rendered markdown. You can read it, follow any wikilink inside it to traverse onward, pop the panel out, or dismiss it.

sociogram.graph.node_selected.q: How do I get back to the full graph?
sociogram.graph.node_selected.a: Dismiss the panel and you are back to the plain graph. Clicking a different node or an edge re-selects rather than returning.

what_is_c2a2.default.q: What are the framings on the What's it doing page?
what_is_c2a2.default.a: Each names an arrangement of agents -- a structure -- and carries one line naming the function that arrangement makes possible. The list is open-ended and grows, so I would rather walk you through them than quote a total.

what_is_c2a2.default.q: Why a set of framings rather than one definition?
what_is_c2a2.default.a: Because no single angle tells the whole story, and the page says exactly that in its own lede. They are a constellation, not a ranking, and none of them reduces to another.

what_is_c2a2.default.q: What is the difference between a structure claim and a function claim here?
what_is_c2a2.default.a: The structure claim names what kind of arrangement the thing is; the function claim says what that arrangement makes possible, in the form 'so it can...'. Same two moves, every framing, without exception.

00_project.a: Infrastructure that lets intellectual and spiritual traditions become visible, interact, and reveal themselves to each other -- a particle accelerator for lineages of thought. It is a concrete response to Alasdair MacIntyre's Gifford-Lectures vision of a university where rival traditions of enquiry are made answerable to one another.

00_project.q: Why is it called an accelerator and detector?
00_project.a: Two halves doing two jobs. The accelerator half brings traditions into contact; the detector half instruments what happens when they meet.

00_project.q: Which traditions are in it, and what do they argue about?
00_project.a: Levin, Friston, Hoffman, Kastrup, McGilchrist, Hawkins, Wolfram, Carroll, Arkani-Hamed, Fredrickson, Stump, Rohr, Wright and Loughran. The questions that recur across programs are whether consciousness is substrate-independent, whether spacetime is fundamental, and the role of attention in constructing reality.

sociogram.graph.edge_selected.q: What does this connection mean, and why are these two linked?
sociogram.graph.edge_selected.a: Clicking an edge shows both endpoint articles, one per panel, so you can see the two nodes a link connects and read why. It is a comparison view rather than a single-node reading.

sociogram.graph.edge_selected.q: How do I read each endpoint, or follow it further?
sociogram.graph.edge_selected.a: Read them side by side, or click a wikilink inside either article to traverse onward. Selecting one endpoint drops you to the single-node view.

sociogram.graph.edge_selected.q: How do I get back to the full graph from here?
sociogram.graph.edge_selected.a: Dismiss, and you are back to the plain graph. Clicking a different edge or node re-selects instead of returning.

what_is_saying.default.q: What does the Saying page mean by what it is saying?
what_is_saying.default.a: It asks what C2A2 communicates as a medium -- what it says by being the shape it is, before it carries any content at all. The worked example the page opens with is a Walkman, which said your music, yours alone, wherever you are, regardless of what was on the tape.

what_is_saying.default.q: How is the Saying lens different from the Doing lens?
what_is_saying.default.a: The Saying lens abstracts from content and reads the thing as a medium. The Doing lens names a structure and the function that structure makes possible. They are a matched pair behind the same question, and neither is a summary of the other.

what_is_saying.default.q: Why these readings, and what is the open card at the end?
what_is_saying.default.a: They are simultaneous readings of one thing, not a ranking and not a league table. The final card is open on purpose, and the page's own claim is that the list cannot close where it stands -- so the list is open-ended, and I would rather walk it with you than give you a number.
